https://www.dailyfreeman.com/2026/08/02/.text: By Elwood Watson PUBLISHED: August 2, 2026 at 12:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Andrew and Tristan Tate, the far-right social media influencers and self-described misogynists who command a following of young, angry men on the internet, were arrested in Miami on July 18 on rape and sex trafficking charges from the United Kingdom. The Tates will be held in custody in Florida as they challenge an extradition claim. British law enforcement announced that the brothers face 59 charges between them, including choking and raping women. Andrew Tate faces further charges relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” Such supplemental charges have been issued to a litany of prior ones, including a 2022 arrest in Romania on rape and sex trafficking; however, that case was dismissed on legal grounds as prosecutors continue to investigate disturbing allegations. Both brothers have denied all wrongdoing, but the allegations paint an abominable portrait of an expansive pornography empire based on physical brutality and a misogynist worldview they feed to boys and young men worldwide. All this creates a high-profile dilemma for the Trump administration. Will President Trump and his affiliates permit the men to be held accountable for their actions, including possible incarceration in the United Kingdom, or will they intervene to protect their allies? The president’s recent comments indicate that he will refrain from intervening in the Tate saga. Time will tell. An in-depth investigation by the New York Times revealed one of Trump’s first actions in his second term in office was arranging the brothers’ return from Romania. Numerous Trump administration officials reportedly persuaded Romanian prosecutors to lift the brothers’ travel restrictions. Additionally, White House officials continued to run interference when customs officials confiscated their devices. The brothers immediately began traveling freely again, arrogantly showing up at parties in cities around the world. It should come as no surprise Andrew Tate was also a longtime admirer of Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein. In a deleted tweet, he once wrote, “EVERYONE wants to be friends with the pimp.” Talk about theater of the perverse. While both Tate brothers have drawn denunciation and scorn across the political spectrum, they have enjoyed empathetic treatment from numerous influential figures on the right. Although the silence among many of these previous supporters is deafening, they do have some detractors . For instance, conservatives such as Megyn Kelly, Ben Shapiro, and Ron DeSantis have been bitter critics of the brothers and have chastised their fellow conservatives who have embraced the duo. By contrast, others on the right have adopted a “hear no evil, fear no evil, see no evil” stance. Sexism and misogyny are not limited to one side of the ideological spectrum. They have deep historical bipartisan roots across organizations of various political stripes, including Young Americans for Freedom , Students for a Democratic Society, The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and The Democratic Socialists of America. Many women who participated were active in these movements early in their existence — the mid-1960s to the early 1970s — spoke of the deeply entrenched sexism and misogyny that pervaded these organizations. We are witnessing such consistent and reductive attitudes with contemporary political outlets, such as Turning Point USA, Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, and similar right wing outlets. As the midterm elections move ever closer, Republicans and a few Democrats seem to be soliciting the manosphere as a vital voting bloc, working under the assumption such an online environment appeals to the vast majority of males. Graham Platner, the supposedly blue collar yet, in reality, prep school misfit, was virtually worshipped as the left’s answer to the manosphere before his eventual demise. Alpha male Gavin Newsom, governor of California and potential 2028 presidential candidate, has consistently decried what he believes is “a crisis of men and masculinity” and has embraced manosphere figures such as Steve Bannon, Ben Shapiro, and the late Charlie Kirk on his podcast. Politics does occasionally make peculiar bedfellows. Whatever President Trump decides, his committed MAGA base will undoubtedly fall in line and accept his choice. Trump has never suffered any significant loss of support for his poor treatment of women or the sexist/misogynist views he shares with the Tate brothers. In fact, he has won the presidency not once but twice in two nonconsecutive terms . Grover Cleveland is the only other president that can claim such a feat. Remember it was Trump who said he “could shoot somebody and wouldn’t lose any voters.” Sadly, given his politically unremitted MAGA base, he is probably correct. Elwood Watson’s column is distributed by Cagle Cartoons newspaper syndicate. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/fierce-in.text: Philip Oltermann in Venice and Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Updated Fri, September 11, 2026 at 5:01 AM UTC 0 Gerda Taro, pictured in Paris in 1936, was one of the first female war photographers, who captured the consequences of war on ordinary people.Photograph: Fred Stein Archive/Getty Images Film premieres at Venice as researchers question who took famous Spanish civil war shot of ‘falling soldier’, credited to the pair’s Robert Capa alias She was one of the most fearless female photojournalists of the 20th century, and the first known to have been killed while covering a war. But in life and in death, the work of Gerda Taro has often been overshadowed by the collaborator and lover whose alias she invented and sometimes shared: Robert Capa. That may be about to change with a new biopic that seeks to pull the pioneering photographer from out of Capa’s shadow, which is premiering at the Venice film festival just as researchers claim to have proof that his most famous and controversial picture was actually taken by her. Taro and Capa were both from middle-class Jewish families – she born in 1910 in Stuttgart under the name Gerta Pohorylle, he three years later in Budapest as Endré Friedmann. Terrified by the rise of Nazism, the two aspiring photojournalists fled to Paris, where their paths crossed and they mingled with other luminaries including Henri Cartier-Bresson, Ernest Hemingway, Martha Gellhorn and Willy Brandt, who would later become Germany’s first postwar social democrat chancellor. It was Taro who came up with a brand name redolent of a seasoned, hard-drinking American war reporter, which they hoped would command respect ( cápa also meaning “shark” in Hungarian) and higher fees. Between 1936 and 1937, the pair covered the Spanish civil war, with pictures taken by both of them published under their alias in the Life and Picture Post magazines. “Gerda Taro both captured the early phase of the Spanish civil war that was still full of optimism and hope, and the tragic final stages,” said Alina Marazzi, the Italian director of the new film La Ragazza Con la Leica (“The Girl With the Leica”), based on Helena Janeczek’s novel of the same name. “She was one of the first women to take pictures from the battlefront, but she also captured the consequences the war had for ordinary people, for women and for children.” Taro’s most widely known series of photographs depicts female militias on a shooting range, one of them shown in iconic profile: kneeling on one knee while steadying a pistol, wearing an overall but also high heels. “It’s such an incredible picture, clearly showing the influence of the Soviet avant garde,” said Marazzi. The showcasing of the feature film in the Venice Lido is taking place amid fresh questions over the most famous photograph to be credited to the Robert Capa alias, which researchers claim may have been taken by Taro and not Capa, as hitherto thought. The Death of a Militiaman gained fame when Life magazine published it in July 1937, with a caption stating that it showed the moment a Republican fighter was shot in the head by Francisco Franco’s forces near Córdoba – a claim that has since been contested. Fernando Penco Valenzuela, a Spanish historian, archaeologist and archivist in the city of Córdoba who has spent years studying Capa’s work, said a technical analysis of the photo – also known as The Falling Soldier – suggests it was in fact shot by Taro’s square-format Reflex-Korelle rather than Friedmann’s rectangular-format 35mm Leica. A 2025 Madrid retrospective curated by Magnum, the agency Capa co-founded in 1947, stated in a caption that although some prints of The Falling Soldier were rectangular, the dimension of others suggested the negative “came from a 6x6 camera”. Related: Furious row erupts over Madrid site of one of Robert Capa’s most important pictures Penco’s research pins down the location where the picture was taken to the village of Espejo in the Cerro Muriano mountain range, on the front near Córdoba in southern Spain on 5 September 1936, at the beginning of the Spanish civil war. In a photograph of Taro the day the couple arrived at Espejo, she is seen wearing the Reflex-Korelle, the camera she bought with her first pay cheque as a photographer. An analysis of the pictures taken by both photographers in Espejo attributes all of the square-format photos to Taro and the rectangular ones to Friedmann. As the militiaman picture is square, Penco argues that it is therefore logical to assume it, too, was taken by Taro. “How is it possible that she didn’t take the photo?” he told the Guardian. “I have no doubt about it whatsoever.” Penco’s findings also fuel speculation that the famous picture may have been staged. “As there was no fighting in the area when it was taken, in my opinion the photo was staged,” he said. Marazzi said it was plausible that Taro took The Falling Soldier picture, which is shown in her film. “We know that around the time the picture was taken, Capa and Taro were often taking pictures in the same places.” Penco said that while it was commonplace at the time for photographers to file in the name of their group or cooperative, the fact that Friedmann and Taro were a couple may have further complicated their attribution. The Girl With the Leica opens at a point where Taro (played by the German actor Emilia Schüle) and Friedmann (played by Aaron Altaras) have retreated back to Paris because the civil war in Spain has become too dangerous. But Taro is restless. “Even though it was her who invented the entire Robert Capa persona, there was a point where she developed a fierce need to be independent,” said Marazzi. “The world sees only Capa, and I’m disappearing behind him,” the actor playing Taro says in the film, before deciding to return to the Iberian peninsula to take more pictures. In July 1937, Taro was photographing fighting in the Brunete region near Madrid for the French communist newspaper Ce Soir when she was run over and crushed by a reversing Republican tank. She died at El Goloso hospital in El Escorial and was later buried at Père-Lachaise cemetery in Paris. https://www.wmtw.com/article/russia-parl.text: Early results from Russia’s first wartime parliamentary election, released by the country’s election commission early Monday, showed the main Kremlin party, United Russia, dominating the vote. The tightly controlled balloting was virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin’s policies and all but certain to cement the Kremlin’s dominance. The vote began Friday for 111 million eligible voters and ended Sunday. The balloting included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began, but still doesn’t fully control, as well as those in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, a move Kyiv denounced as illegal and the European Union described as a “blatant violation of international law.” With some 58% of the precincts counted, United Russia had nearly 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies apportioned by party lists, according to Russia’s Central Election Commission. Another 225 lawmakers will be chosen in single-seat races, and United Russia also was poised to win most of those. As the early results came in, voting continued at some embassies and consulates in time zones further west, including in the United States. Kremlin long expected to keep control The Kremlin has sought the parliamentary election — the first since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — to showcase popular support for the war and legitimize its action. It has sought to avoid political risks by stamping out any dissent. A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election in the absence of genuine opposition all but assure the Kremlin will keep tight control of Russian politics amid mounting economic costs and increasing Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country. Voters cast two separate ballots, filling half of the Duma’s 450 seats by selecting political parties listed on the ballot. The rest are contested in single-seat constituencies, with voters choosing individual candidates. The main Kremlin party, United Russia, has been widely expected to retain its overwhelming control of the lower house, the State Duma. The early results showed four other parties that almost always vote for Kremlin initiatives returning to the State Duma. Opposition sidelined as observers report violations The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court, and only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races. Additionally, some anti-war politicians were imprisoned or forced to flee abroad ahead of the campaign. Yabloko and the Communist Party, which has criticized some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of Putin, said many of their observers were turned away from polling stations. Russia didn’t invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, with the Russian Foreign Ministry accusing the body of “double standards” for its criticism of Russia. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said that the decision was a breach of Russia’s commitments as a member state of the organization. Yabloko reported that one of its observers lost consciousness while being arrested by police at a St. Petersburg polling station on Saturday, after officials accused him of trying to “disrupt the elections” and called police. The parties reported violations including sealed ballot boxes being opened, doors to polling stations not being secured overnight, and a refusal to issue paper ballots. The claims could not be independently verified. At one polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box as an armed Russian soldier stood nearby and watched. Issues with electronic voting in Moscow Ella Pamfilova, head of Russia’s Central Election Commission, said Sunday that the electronic voting system in Moscow was targeted by cyberattacks. She blamed one of the “systemic parties” — meaning one of those taking part in the vote, without specifying which one. SotaVision, an independent Russian news outlet, said Sunday that voters were reporting glitches in the electronic registry systems at polling stations across Moscow. People were not issued paper ballots and instead were asked to vote via an electronic terminal, the outlet said on Telegram. Leonid Volkov, a close associate of the late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, suggested the supposed breakdown of the system used to issue paper ballots in Moscow may have been deliberate, aimed at pushing voters toward electronic voting. “Demand a paper ballot!” he wrote on X on Sunday. Lines formed outside polling stations as many voters refused to vote electronically. Having urged supporters to spoil party-list ballots, Yabloko party leader Nikolai Rybakov cast a ballot in St. Petersburg on Sunday, covered in bright green writing declaring “For freedom," “For peace,” and “Yabloko.” Russian opposition abroad holds protests Russia’s exiled opposition, including the widow of Alexei Navalny, Yulia Navalnaya, called on anti-war Russians to cast their votes at noon on Sunday. Thousands of Russians living in Armenia took part in the vote, lining up outside the Russian Embassy in the capital, Yerevan. Some of them joined the “Noon for a Peaceful Russia” anti-war demonstration, holding anti-war and anti-Putin posters. Mark Podberezin, a journalist, said members of the election commission in Yerevan made remarks that felt like “outright intimidation.” He said he had heard comments "along the lines of, ‘You’ll have to return to Russia sooner or later, keep that in mind.’” Lidiya Klimenko said she did not think her vote would have any real impact. The most useful thing to do, she said, was “to see other people who are also against the war, to be together in a shared cause.” In Germany, voters cast their ballots at the Russian Embassy in Berlin. Andrei Pivovarov, a dissident and former head of the Open Russia group, addressed a protest gathered outside the building. Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia The election's last day came against a backdrop of a major wave of Ukrainian attacks. Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces shot down a total of 1,110 Ukrainian drones across Russia, as well as over the annexed Crimea and the Black Sea. Two people were killed and 20 wounded across the wider Moscow region, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The election follows a summer of Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes on oil refineries that triggered a widespread fuel crisis. Warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon also were attacked. Those attacks have exacerbated economic problems and brought the war home for millions.
